repos.title: Trainspotting: Learning Object-Centric 3D Reconstruction from Found Photos
repos.paper_summary: Trainspotting is a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons, reconstructed to provide camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks, along with a fine-tuned feedforward model, Spotter, built from VGGT-Ω. Each object is reconstructed by filtering photos with SAM3 prompts, matching image pairs with RoMa v2 under confidence, cycle-consistency, and epipolar checks, running COLMAP, selecting views by covisibility, and running Cas-DiffMVS depth verified against MoGe-2. Spotter is fine-tuned on training objects with a camera, depth, and point loss, with 15% replay from BlendedMVS, Hypersim, and uCO3D. On 1,000 held-out objects, camera-pose AUC@30 rises from 25.0 to 81.2 over VGGT-Ω, and on NAVI in-the-wild from 19 to 76. Depth AbsRel falls from 0.201 to 0.071. Performance on conventional benchmarks is largely unchanged. Limitations: the regime labels come from LLM classification and are approximate, and structure from motion succeeds for only 85% of objects.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Public archives hold many found photos of one object, but feedforward reconstruction models are trained mostly on single-session captures.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing object datasets record each object in one capture, and internet photo reconstructions cover mostly scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: The Trainspotting Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: Language-model classification of Wikimedia Commons categories yields 12,068 rigid objects, each labeled fixed, roaming, or instance-pooled.

digest_headlines.heading: Pseudo-Ground Truth via Reconstruction
digest_headlines.headline: A dense-matching pipeline with geometric checks recovers camera poses, depth, and masks for each object as pseudo-ground truth.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning lifts held-out camera-pose score at the 30-degree threshold from 25.0 to 81.2 and depth inlier ratio from 28.1 to 53.3.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Variation in how an object is photographed, not only dataset scale, is what the base models lacked.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists category counts, rejected categories, pipeline yields, matcher comparison, thresholds, training, and evaluation details.

repos.title: A Unified Fractal Impedance Control Framework
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents H-PMP, a controller that nests a task-space admittance or HapFIC controller inside a joint-space HapFIC. It also presents the FIC Suite, an open-source toolkit with ROS2, MuJoCo, and hardware drivers for Fractal Impedance Controllers (FIC). The task layer maps the desired pose and external wrench to joint torques through the Jacobian transpose. The joint layer applies the FIC effort function, whose saturations bound the admittance offset so the controller moves between admittance and impedance behaviour. The Suite offers a desktop and web GUI, live tuning of effort profiles, and a 1 kHz robot node. A new robot needs a driver and a YAML file. On a Kinova Gen3, three experiments (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) compare H-PMP with earlier FIC architectures. The excerpt reports no tracking-error, force, or timing values from these runs, so the claim of no computational overhead has no measured support there. The conclusion's efficiency argument compares the MCU's rated maximum power (about 400 mW) with a 15 to 17 W board, not a measured run. Online adaptive tuning is stated as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Robots in unstructured settings need interaction control that trades admittance against impedance, and this paper packages FIC into one library.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Redundant robots were restricted to one mode, and earlier trade-off methods risked instability, which FIC addresses through passivity.

digest_headlines.heading: The FIC Suite
digest_headlines.headline: One FIC Studio graphical interface drives MuJoCo simulation and vendor hardware through the same library and profile files, tested so far on two arms.

digest_headlines.heading: FIC Controllers
digest_headlines.headline: H-PMP nests a task-space admittance controller inside a joint-space FIC layer, with a shared FIC effort function underneath.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Validation
digest_headlines.headline: Three experiments on a Kinova Gen3 arm compare H-PMP with three other FIC architectures on tracking, contact loss and demonstration.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: H-PMP balances impedance and admittance, and the authors name adaptive online tuning as the next step.

repos.title: Terminal-style Mathematical Modeling Bench: The First Agentic and Verifiable Benchmark for Mathematical Modeling
repos.paper_summary: TB-MathModel is a benchmark of 18 real CUMCM and MCM modeling problems from 2023–2025, run in a containerized terminal, where an agent must return one JSON artifact. The artifact's numeric core is scored against a panel of human outstanding papers, with one vote per paper. A feasibility gate zeroes infeasible answers and is backed by 624 Lean 4 certificate obligations. Scoring is one-sided: meeting or beating the anchor never scores below 1.0. Across seven multimodal entries with three seeds each, GPT-6 Astra + codex scores 64.58% O-Eval (±2.93), Fable 5.1 + claude-code scores 63.11% (±1.33), and DeepSeek-Flash + opencode scores 59.81% (±1.25) at USD 2.54 per pass, against USD 246.41 for the top entry. Changing only the harness moves O-Eval by at most 0.07 pp. Limitations: per-seed deviations reach 2.93 pp, so adjacent rows are not significantly separated; the feasibility layers cannot verify physical truth unless a problem admits an independent replay; literature-split tasks are excluded from headline rankings; and panels range from 1 to 18 papers per task.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks miss modeling; TB-MathModel is the first to make full contest problems agentic, verifiable and terminal.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier modeling benchmarks score a single solver artifact or an LLM-judged report, and none is agentic, verifiable and terminal.

digest_headlines.heading: The TB-MathModel Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: Scoring against a panel of outstanding papers, with one-sided rewards and a feasibility gate, defines the benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The newest flagships top seven multimodal entries, while a 2.54 USD open model reaches 59.81 at about 1/100 the cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: TB-MathModel gives a reproducible, machine-checkable signal, and its two-layer feasibility design is the transferable idea.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Modeling has no single correct answer, so panel sizes range from 1 to 18 papers and literature-split tasks are excluded from headline rankings.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Official outstanding-paper solutions are not redistributed, and users should confirm licence terms before redistributing the material.

digest_headlines.heading: Use of Large Language Models
digest_headlines.headline: Language models were both the systems under test and drafting aids, while the authors specified and verified all benchmark components.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset composition, environment, per-entry configuration, scoring formulas, and the Lean obligation catalogue.

repos.title: VerdictAD: Few-Shot Anomaly Detection via Decision-Guided Refinement
repos.paper_summary: VerdictAD is a training-free framework that refines the outputs of existing few-shot anomaly detectors using decisions from a frozen typed decision model (Clef-Flash, which outputs binary decision probabilities without text generation). Its Global Verdict Refinement (GVR) gates the image-level score by the averaged reference-free and reference-conditioned decision logits. Its Local Verdict Refinement (LVR) scores overlapping windows with crop and red-box views, averages these probabilities into a verification map, and multiplies the anomaly map by it, so it can only reweight existing responses. The base detector is a frozen DINOv2-L nearest-neighbor patch method, with max pooling for the image score. On MVTec AD, VisA, and MVTec LOCO AD, the paper reports image-level and pixel-level AUROC, AUPR, and AUPRO for 1-, 2-, and 4-shot settings. In the 1-shot setting, DINOv2-L + Ours reaches 97.5% image AUROC on MVTec AD and 95.7% on VisA, against 94.3% and 92.0% for the base DINOv2-L. AnomalyDINO + Ours and SubspaceAD + Ours also improve over their baselines in the reported rows. Limitations stated by the paper: the method cannot recover anomaly evidence absent from the original detector, and LVR's gains depend on the base map already containing useful signal.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Few-shot anomaly detectors often flag normal variations and may miss logical defects, so VerdictAD adds typed visual decisions to refine their scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior few-shot methods mostly change feature representations or use vision-language prompts, while typed decision models remain unexplored for anomaly detection.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: VerdictAD multiplies existing anomaly scores and maps by probabilities from a frozen typed decision model, without changing the base detector.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Refinement lifts image-level scores on MVTec LOCO AD at four shots, for example PatchCore rising from 67.4 to 78.0.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion finds the gains strongest for logical anomalies, but refinement cannot recover evidence absent from the base detector.

digest_headlines.heading: LLM Usage Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the language-model assistance used for editing, formatting and table preparation, and the authors' verification of results.

repos.title: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs
repos.paper_summary:
H2RB is a human-robot co-training framework that adapts pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies using unpaired human and robot demonstrations. It uses a decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer, which has a shared encoder mapping human and robot wrist-hand action chunks into one latent space with separate decoders per embodiment, and geometry-anchored alignment, an auxiliary loss that regresses wrist pose and five fingertip positions from mean-pooled VLM features. A flow-matching policy predicts the latents.

On OpenArm, object transfer scores are 8.0 for the human-only base policy and 51.8 for H2RB, versus 27.2 for the Ego-Pi shared-action baseline (20 in-distribution and 10 out-of-distribution rollouts per object). Skill transfer on opening and closing is 0.0 for the Ego-Pi and HaWoR shared-action baselines and 62.7 for H2RB. Out-of-distribution object transfer under placement shift rises from 6.0 to 45.3. The tokenizer raises skill transfer from 0.0 to 49.7, and cross-domain latent regularization lowers the normalized human-robot latent gap from 3.81 to 1.53. On RB-Y1 parcel orientation over 50 trials, success rises from 64% (robot-only) to 78% with heterogeneous training and geometry grounding.

Results come from a single robot platform with few rollouts per condition.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Target-robot demonstrations are costly, so the paper proposes adapting pretrained robot policies using human demonstrations.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: H2RB pairs a shared latent action tokenizer with separate decoders and grounds vision-language features in hand geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: H2RB scores 62.7 on skill transfer where shared-action co-training baselines score 0.0 on both skills.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Latent alignment reduces the human-robot latent gap from 3.81 to 1.53 and preserves faster human-demonstrated motion.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior alignment methods rely on paired demonstrations, trajectory pseudo-pairs, or synthesized robot-domain images.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: H2RB improves human-to-robot transfer and robot-only adaptation, with further gains from heterogeneous training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, tokenizer and loss definitions, heterogeneous training data, and a parcel-handling evaluation protocol.

repos.title: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
repos.paper_summary:
RoboTryOn converts egocentric human manipulation videos into robot demonstrations with action labels, treating human-to-robot transfer as virtual try-on: the human motion is kept and the human is replaced by a target robot shown in a reference image. Three flow-matching models are trained on robot data only. An image model inpaints selected human keyframes into robot keyframes, conditioned on an arm mask, a hand skeleton, and the previous robot keyframe. A video model interpolates between keyframes under hand skeleton flow. An inverse dynamics model predicts joint-space actions, and inverse kinematics corrects the wrist positions. A vision-language-action policy is then trained on the synthetic data, alone or together with teleoperated data.

Evaluation uses two bimanual robots with dexterous hands and eleven tabletop tasks. Four in-domain tasks have 50 teleoperated demonstrations and 50 human videos per robot; seven out-of-domain tasks have only human videos. Averaged over both robots, out-of-domain success rises from 2.1% to 60.0%, and bimanual tasks reach 45.9%. Training on synthetic data matches teleoperation-only policies at about one third of the collection cost.

Limitations: only two robots and eleven tasks were tested, and imperfect hand retargeting is handled by perturbing and dropping skeleton inputs during training.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Human videos differ from robot demonstrations in appearance and action, and RoboTryOn is proposed to translate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior human-video methods retarget, render, or translate footage, while this work adds action labels for policy learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A three-stage pipeline translates human keyframes into robot keyframes, synthesizes robot video, and labels actions with an inverse dynamics model.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Adding synthetic demonstrations to teleoperated ones raised OpenArm out-of-domain success from 3.1% to 73.0%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Synthesized demonstrations teach seven tasks without robot demonstrations, matching teleoperation at about a third of its cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists limitations and future work, implementation details, per-task results, and figure captions for the experiments.

repos.title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes
repos.paper_summary: GFlowQEC is a generative flow network (GFlowNet) that proposes quantum LDPC codes. To the authors' knowledge, it is the first GFlowNet for quantum code design. It builds a lifted-product code one group element per slot and is trained with trajectory balance, so each code is sampled with probability proportional to a power of its failure-exponent score. The policy is trained once on scores from 42 earlier runs, then frozen. At 180 physical qubits, ranking ten policy draws per paid call finds 2.4 and 2.8 times as many new top-scoring codes, inequivalent to training codes, as tuned parallel tempering at noise biases γ = ±1. It finds over 3.5 times as many as a supervised screen. A screen ranking a hundred random candidates per call beats the policy. Soft Q-learning does as well at one bias and better at the other. Limitations: the gain is in codes found per budget, not the best code, since no code beats those from Bayesian optimisation, reinforcement learning or LLM searches. Scores use code distances only, with no decoder, and stored data and training are uncounted.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Good quantum codes are rare and each evaluation is costly, so a learned proposer may yield more good codes per call.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior searches include strong simple baselines, and GFlowNets have so far been applied to circuits rather than codes.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Lifted-product codes over a 36-element group give 180 physical qubits from ten group elements.

digest_headlines.heading: Search Space and Oracle
digest_headlines.headline: Codes are scored by a failure exponent from their distances, with a top-scoring threshold of 10.0 at bias plus or minus one.

digest_headlines.heading: GFlowQEC
digest_headlines.headline: GFlowQEC builds each tuple one slot at a time and trains on stored scores with no new oracle calls.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The policy is compared with tuned parallel tempering, a supervised screen, soft Q-learning and other searches at matched budgets.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: The policy finds 2.4 and 2.8 times as many inequivalent top-scoring codes as tuned parallel tempering; a screen wins at a hundred draws.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The lead holds per paid call but vanishes per CPU second of exact ladders.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A frozen policy finds more inequivalent top-scoring codes per paid call, but circuit-level noise remains untested.

repos.title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure
repos.paper_summary: EDGAR is a diffusion-based refinement framework that corrects artifacts in Gaussian head avatars and then distills the refined renderings back into the avatar. The method adapts the one-step SD-Turbo backbone with a Sapiens identity-feature fusion block, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router with six experts, and an expression loss on POSTER V2 features. It is trained on EDGAR-SET, a triplet dataset of degraded renderings, ground-truth frames, and reference images built from real NeRSemble captures (99 identities) and synthetic CAFCA avatars (1,500 identities), with about half of pairs filtered by LPIPS. The refined multi-view renders then supervise a single Gaussian avatar with L1 and SSIM losses, so the final avatar renders without EDGAR and without added Gaussians. Experiments on CAP4D, GaussianAvatars, and RGBAvatar compare against raw outputs and an SDEdit-style baseline, reporting perceptual and reconstruction gains, cross-view consistency, and tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions. Limitations: the training data covers only recoverable degradations, severe structural errors in unobserved regions remain, and mean temporal error (tWE) rose for GaussianAvatars.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Monocular Gaussian avatars show artifacts, so EDGAR refines degraded renderings with a diffusion prior and reference identity.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior refinement methods use SDEdit-style noising that can alter identity, while EDGAR adds reference features and paired supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: EDGAR-SET pairs simulated degraded renderings with ground truth and reference images, and EDGAR injects Sapiens features into a one-step diffusion model.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Against raw inputs and SDEdit, EDGAR leads most self-reenactment metrics, and 15 participants preferred it.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: EDGAR's gains vary by pipeline and metric, and severe structural errors in unobserved regions can remain.

repos.title: Crop Mapping Evaluation under Sampling Bias
repos.paper_summary:
This paper applies a weighted form of prediction-powered inference (PPI) to estimate a crop map's macro-F1 across its deployment region when field labels are a biased sample. Propensity weights, from an XGBoost model that separates labeled from unlabeled parcels, give more weight to under-sampled conditions and correct the classifier's errors on labeled parcels.

Using five European regions where crop registers label every declared parcel, the authors simulate six documented collection practices, which create gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1. Under each region's worst-case rule, 5 km block cross-validation overestimates macro-F1 by up to 0.18, while PPI with satellite-embedding weights reduces the largest error to 0.07. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights is nearly as accurate. On the Kenyan roadside Helmets dataset, PPI lowers the estimate from 0.93 (random CV) to 0.61, but this correction relies on a few heavily weighted labels.

Limitations: the European regions were chosen to produce large gaps, the experiments cover one binary task and one collection rule at a time, and the 95% intervals contain the true value in fewer than 95% of runs.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Field labels come from accessible places, so cross-validation on them can overstate crop map performance across the region.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Weighted prediction-powered inference estimates region-wide macro-F1 from biased labels, with weights from a propensity model.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Across all rules and regions, PPI with embedding weights cuts absolute mean error from 0.053 to 0.016.

digest_headlines.heading: Case study: three Kenyan datasets
digest_headlines.headline: On the roadside Helmets dataset, weighted correction lowers estimated macro-F1 from 0.93 to 0.61, though it rests on few heavily weighted labels.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: Spatial cross-validation methods do not consistently close the gap, so reporting weighted estimates with intervals is recommended.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the European and Kenyan label summaries, collection-rule formulas, interval derivation, campaign workflow, and Helmets land-cover analysis.

repos.title: TEXMET: A Deep Learning Benchmark for Archaeological Textile Reconstruction
repos.paper_summary: TEXMET is a curated dataset of 18,644 historical textile images from the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Open Access collection, with a benchmark evaluating three puzzle-solving models (JPDVT, FCViT, DiffAssemble) on regular 3×3 grid puzzles. Images were collected through the MET REST API, filtered with CLIP embeddings, UMAP clustering and manual quality review, and split 14,915 / 1,864 / 1,865 for train, validation and test. The models were trained on synthetic puzzles cut from intact textile images. Pre-trained transformer models did not transfer: FCViT dropped from a 56.61%-level ImageNet baseline to 8.30% on TEXMET, and JPDVT fell from 67.89% to 32.92%. DiffAssemble kept its performance across the shift (65.08% on TEXMET against 56.61% on ImageNet). Fine-tuned DiffAssemble reached 85.89% puzzle accuracy on textile data. On 45 degraded Oseberg fragments, accuracy rose from 26.67% to 64.44% after fine-tuning. Limitations: evaluation covers only regular grids without rotation, Oseberg fragments are artificially split into 3×3 patches because no ground truth exists, and the sample is 45 fragments.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Oseberg textile fragments lack a textile puzzle benchmark, so the authors build TEXMET and test three puzzle models.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier puzzle work targeted clean pieces, and no prior study evaluated modern deep models on historical textiles.

digest_headlines.heading: The TEXMET Dataset
digest_headlines.headline: TEXMET holds 18,644 Metropolitan Museum textile images after the authors removed 8,716 poor or noisy samples.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Three puzzle models are described: JPDVT as diffusion, FCViT as coordinate regression, and DiffAssemble as graph diffusion.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are tested on ImageNet, TEXMET and 45 Oseberg fragments, with seeded splits and single runs per configuration.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning DiffAssemble lifts Oseberg puzzle accuracy from 26.67% to 64.44%, while JPDVT and FCViT do not adapt.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors attribute DiffAssemble's advantage to its graph structure and argue that missing training data, not architecture, limited transfer.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that domain fine-tuning is essential, while irregular shapes and cross-fragment matching remain open.
